items.title: Johnny Lala Interview, 1960-03-15
items.q: Tom came down here and wanted to get bands to go up there. He wanted to be a big shot.

ctx.x: I used to get up there.

I used to get up there. I used to get up there. I was like a monkey. I would keep my mind shut. And I was getting the money. So you all, man, go fight. Make a fool out of yourself. I was getting the money. I was getting the money. If the father would tell me, if he'd tell me that this, this pussy was black, I'd say, yeah, you were right. You were wrong. But this father wouldn't argue. I wouldn't argue with nobody. Hmm. You're right. But they wouldn't argue. They wouldn't tell the man that's standing, the man…

Deacon Lawyer, Ken, made a classical remark. He always tells you about the old days. You know that, Raymond? I mean, I'm on a job. He always tells you about the old days. I'm on a job. No, yeah, when they call a Deacon. Yeah, he was up there. And we were talking about Tom. He was saying about, in the early days, people before Tom Brown went to Chicago, you know? And somebody in the group, or maybe it was myself, said, well, according to the records, you know, Tom Brown was the first one who took a white band to…

items.title: Johnny Lala Interview, 1958-09-24
items.q: Then from there, what was Tom Brown? Tom Brown grabbed ahold of me. After Tom Brown grabbed ahold of me.

ctx.x: And did your father play ragtime?

Well, in them days there was what you call, it wasn't ragtime in them days. My father did. You know, it was dance fans, you know, but there wasn't no pep, you know? It was a regular, legitimate resistance, you see? Of course, they played with what was called ragtime in them days, but none of them was out there the Negroes. You see, my daddy gave it up. My daddy gave up music out when I was about ten years old, you see? You know, I'll never forget I was a young kid. First time I stood out all night, played with a…
I'm not going to be a man. I'm not going to be a man. I'm not going to be a man. I'm not going to be a man.
